## 0253. Describe PROMETHEUS and the system boundaries it uses.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Category | model descriptions and methods |
| Route | `model_explanation` |
| Route reason | named-model metadata request |
| Qwen generations | 0 |
| Time | 0.07 s |
| Conversation | standalone |

**Full answer**

### PROMETHEUS

Description:
The Prometheus model is a comprehensive world energy model with innovative features: it integrates stochastic relations and so all exogenous variables – parameters are stochastic, following explicit probability distributions, including covariance. Therefore, all model results are also stochastic (probability distributions). Among others, stochastic distributions are used for technology change and learning by doing, as well as for fossil fuel resources, both conventional and unconventional. Prometheus models the world energy system divided into 10 regions and produces yearly projections up to 2050; the update to 2070 is ongoing. The model includes a set of long time series (IEA data mostly) on which econometric estimations are carried out. The model produces projections of energy demand by sector (industry, domestic, transport), power generation (representing about 25 technologies), RES, and hydrogen supply and use. Prometheus puts emphasis on oil and gas resources, while coal is assumed to have rather abundant supplies relative to production prospects in the projection time horizon. The model incorporates uncertainty surrounding the amount of oil and gas resources that are yet to be discovered. Data are mostly calibrated on estimation of resources by USGS. The model produces projections of fossil fuel prices, which depend on demand, supply, technology and resources. As all outputs are probabilistic, fossil fuel price projections take the form of probability distributions. The model includes CO2 emissions and can simulate emission reduction pathways.

Developer:
E3Modelling S.A. https://e3modelling.com/

Related model documentation:
- [IAM PARIS model page](https://iamparis.eu/models/55)

| Route reason | named-model metadata request |
| Qwen generations | 0 |
| Time | 0.06 s |
| Conversation | standalone |

**Full answer**

### GEM-E3

Description:
The GEM-E3 model is a multi-regional, multi-sectoral, recursive dynamic computable general equilibrium (CGE) model which provides details on the macro-economy and its interaction with the environment and the energy system. It is an empirical, large scale model, written entirely in structural form. GEM-E3 allows for a consistent comparative analysis of policy scenarios since it ensures that in all scenarios, the economic system remains in general equilibrium. In addition, it incorporates micro-economic mechanisms and institutional features within a consistent macro-economic framework and avoids the representation of behaviour in reduced form. Particularly valuable are the insights the model provides regarding the distributional aspects of long-term structural adjustments. The GEM-E3 model is extensively used as a tool of policy analysis and impact assessment.

Developer:
E3Modelling - RICARDO

Related model documentation:
- [IAM PARIS model page](https://iamparis.eu/models/75)

**Full answer**

### EnergyPLAN

Description:
EnergyPLAN is an input-output model that simulates the annual operation of the entire energy system in hourly time steps. It includes electricity, heating, cooling, transport, industry and desalination demands. For production it includes various types of power plants, variable renewable energy sources and combined heat and power plants. The main focus is to be able to simulate smart energy systems, and therefore includes modelling of electricity, district heating and gas grids. It allows for many types of P2X applications both for heating, gas and liquid fuels.

Developer:
Sustainable Energy Planning Group, Aalborg University

- [IAM PARIS model page](https://iamparis.eu/models/22)

**Full answer**

### OSeMOSYS

Description:
The Open Source energy MOdelling SYStem – OSeMOSYS is a long-term energy and resource planning tool that stands for an open, transparent and accessible approach of energy planning. It is a bottom-up linear optimization modelling system. In the last few years OSeMOSYS has already been used to build regional models like the The Electricity Model Base for Africa – TEMBA, and The open source South American Model Base – SAMBA. In the Horizon 2020 EU REEEM project the Open Source energy Modelling Base for the European Union – OSeMBE was developed. OSeMOSYS has a low learning threshold and is available in three modelling languages (Python, GAMS and GNU MathProg), fitting the needs of different communities of users. That allowed its spread in numerous countries worldwide, for academic research, capacity development and support to national planning processes.

Developer:
KTH

Related model documentation:
- [IAM PARIS model page](https://iamparis.eu/models/52)

**Full answer**

### AIM/Enduse India 3.3

Description:
The AIM/End-use Indian model integrates the water module at the resource and technological level into the existing energy and environment systems (Vishwanathan et al 2017, 2018a, Vishwanathan and Garg 2020) to capture the impacts of existing and future policies for water, energy, and land systems on the major water- and energy-intensive sectors. The model uses recursive dynamics and runs in annual time steps. It optimizes costs (technology, energy, and water) and resources (water, energy) by selecting a set of best available technologies based on given physical resources and technological and environmental parameters. A detailed characterization of the inputs reflects an optimistic engineering view of technological progress. Economic parameters, such as taxes, subsidies, resource (energy, water, and land) technologies, policies, and social costs are also classified. The final service demand is exogenous, and is driven not only by the gross domestic product (GDP) but also by end-use consumption and policies across various sub-sectors. The model is also being soft-linked to climatic–hydrological models (Vishwanathan et al 2018b).

Developer:
Indian Institute of Management Ahmedabad

Related model documentation:
- [IAM PARIS model page](https://iamparis.eu/models/5)

### AIM/Enduse India 3.3

Description:
The AIM/End-use Indian model integrates the water module at the resource and technological level into the existing energy and environment systems (Vishwanathan et al 2017, 2018a, Vishwanathan and Garg 2020) to capture the impacts of existing and future policies for water, energy, and land systems on the major water- and energy-intensive sectors. The model uses recursive dynamics and runs in annual time steps. It optimizes costs (technology, energy, and water) and resources (water, energy) by selecting a set of best available technologies based on given physical resources and technological and environmental parameters. A detailed characterization of the inputs reflects an optimistic engineering view of technological progress. Economic parameters, such as taxes, subsidies, resource (energy, water, and land) technologies, policies, and social costs are also classified. The final service demand is exogenous, and is driven not only by the gross domestic product (GDP) but also by end-use consumption and policies across various sub-sectors. The model is also being soft-linked to climatic–hydrological models (Vishwanathan et al 2018b).

Developer:
Indian Institute of Management Ahmedabad

Related model documentation:
- [IAM PARIS model page](https://iamparis.eu/models/5)

<a id="q0431"></a>

## 0431. Explain the difference between a carbon budget and an annual CO2 target in IAM results.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Category | conceptual explanation |
| Route | `general_qa` |
| Route reason | conceptual climate explanation |
| Qwen generations | 1 |
| Time | 1.67 s |
| Conversation | standalone |

**Full answer**

A carbon budget is the maximum cumulative net CO₂ emissions allowed under a given warming target, measured from a reference date. An annual CO₂ target is a specific estimate of emissions for a year, which may be part of the broader carbon budget. The difference lies in the scope: the budget accounts for the total emissions over time, while the annual target is a yearly estimate. (Source: IPCC AR6 glossary)

## 0433. Why does the distinction between a carbon budget and an annual CO2 target matter for climate-policy analysis?

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Category | conceptual explanation |
| Route | `general_qa` |
| Route reason | conceptual climate explanation |
| Qwen generations | 1 |
| Time | 0.79 s |
| Conversation | standalone |

**Full answer**

The distinction between a carbon budget and an annual CO2 target matters for climate-policy analysis because the carbon budget represents the cumulative maximum emissions allowed under a given warming target, while the annual CO2 target specifies the emissions level for a specific year. This distinction helps policymakers understand the long-term and cumulative impacts of climate action, guiding decisions on policy frameworks, funding, and implementation strategies.

<a id="q0435"></a>

## 0435. Explain the difference between gross emissions and net emissions in IAM results.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Category | conceptual explanation |
| Route | `general_qa` |
| Route reason | conceptual climate explanation |
| Qwen generations | 1 |
| Time | 0.80 s |
| Conversation | standalone |

**Full answer**

In IAM results, **gross emissions** include all carbon dioxide (CO₂) emissions, such as from agriculture, forestry, and other land use, and do not account for removals from the atmosphere (e.g., biochar). **Net emissions** subtract these removals, providing a more accurate measure of net CO₂ flux.

<a id="q0436"></a>

The installed power capacity (available electricity generation capacity) is the total installed electricity generation capacity reported in the IAM results, while the generated electricity refers to the actual electricity produced by the systems in question. The difference lies in the time frame: installed capacity is the current or past value, whereas generated electricity is the actual electricity produced at that time. Both are part of the IAM model's assessment of electricity generation and infrastructure.

**Full answer**

In IAM results, a carbon price reflects the cost of reducing the last tonne of CO₂ needed to meet a target, influenced by factors like technology costs, fuel switching options, economic structures, and baseline emissions. A lower carbon price indicates a model assumes cheaper low-carbon technologies, while a higher price reflects more complex scenarios. A carbon tax, though a policy tool, is not explicitly mentioned in IAM results but is a key driver of carbon pricing models.

## 0455. Explain the difference between negative emissions and avoided emissions in IAM results.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Category | conceptual explanation |
| Route | `general_qa` |
| Route reason | conceptual climate explanation |
| Qwen generations | 1 |
| Time | 1.07 s |
| Conversation | standalone |

**Full answer**

Negative emissions and avoided emissions in IAM results refer to two distinct aspects of climate mitigation. Avoided emissions are the net reductions in greenhouse gas emissions that would otherwise occur, such as from sectors like aviation, shipping, and agriculture. Negative emissions, on the other hand, are the net emissions that are generated by actions like carbon removal (CDR) or net-negative emissions (NNE) that offset the emissions from sectors that are hard to abate. These two concepts are used to assess the effectiveness of different mitigation strategies in achieving climate goals.

The key difference lies in their purpose and the level of certainty: projections are conditional and uncertain, while observations are direct and measurable.

| Time | 0.79 s |

**Full answer**

A historical calibration in IAM results refers to the process of adjusting past data to align with future projections, while a future projection is the hypothetical outcome of assuming current and future conditions. Calibration helps refine the accuracy of IAM results by aligning them with historical data, whereas projections represent the hypothetical impact of current and future assumptions on climate and energy outcomes.

**Full answer**

In IAM results, **renewable generation** refers to the actual output of renewable energy sources (e.g., wind, solar, hydro) and is treated as low-carbon because they absorb CO₂ during production. **Renewable capacity** refers to the total amount of renewable energy available, which is limited by land, competition with food production, and sustainability constraints. IAM models use these to assess the feasibility and impact of renewable energy on climate mitigation.

## 0515. Explain the difference between carbon removal and carbon capture in IAM results.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Category | conceptual explanation |
| Route | `general_qa` |
| Route reason | conceptual climate explanation |
| Qwen generations | 1 |
| Time | 1.01 s |
| Conversation | standalone |

**Full answer**

Carbon capture (CCS) captures CO₂ at industrial sources and stores it underground, reducing emissions but not removing CO₂ from the atmosphere. Carbon removal (CDR) like afforestation or BECCS removes CO₂ from the atmosphere, balancing residual emissions from sectors like aviation or industry. In IAM results, CCS limits emissions from hard-to-abate sectors, while CDR helps offset remaining emissions, though CDR's effectiveness varies by model and scenario.

The effectiveness of each method depends on factors like land availability, cost, and feasibility, which are critical for policy decisions.

## 0519. Explain the difference between a technology cost and a system cost in IAM results.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Category | conceptual explanation |
| Route | `general_qa` |
| Route reason | conceptual climate explanation |
| Qwen generations | 1 |
| Time | 1.26 s |
| Conversation | standalone |

**Full answer**

In IAM results, a **technology cost** refers to the cost of adopting a specific technology (e.g., solar PV, wind, or batteries) as its cumulative deployment grows, often described by a learning rate. A **system cost** includes the combined costs of all technologies, including infrastructure, energy production, and other systems involved in achieving the climate goals. The key difference is that technology cost focuses on individual technologies, while system cost considers the entire ecosystem of technologies and systems driving the climate goals.

A higher system cost might indicate the complexity or scale of the implementation, which can affect how much policy is needed to achieve climate goals.

### GCAM

Description:
GCAM is an integrated assessment model that represents interactions among energy, economy, land, water and climate systems. It is commonly used for scenario analysis of emissions, energy transitions and climate policy.

Developer:
Joint Global Change Research Institute

Model scope:
- energy
- economy
- land
- water
- climate

Useful for:
- emissions and energy pathway analysis
- climate policy scenarios
- land and resource interactions
- regional mitigation comparisons

Interpretation notes:
- model assumptions vary by scenario and input dataset
- local IAM PARIS metadata may not include detailed assumptions

### MESSAGEix-GLOBIOM

Description:
MESSAGEix-GLOBIOM is an integrated assessment framework combining the MESSAGEix energy-system model with GLOBIOM land-use and agriculture components. It is used for energy, land, emissions and climate mitigation pathway analysis.

Model scope:
- energy
- land use
- agriculture
- emissions
- climate

Useful for:
- energy-land-climate mitigation pathways
- technology and resource constraints
- emissions trajectories across sectors
- scenario analysis for climate policy

Interpretation notes:
- results depend on scenario protocol and regional aggregation
- local IAM PARIS metadata may not expose all model internals

| Route reason | named-model metadata request |
| Qwen generations | 0 |
| Time | 0.06 s |
| Conversation | c17 |

**Full answer**

### EnergyPLAN

Description:
EnergyPLAN is an input-output model that simulates the annual operation of the entire energy system in hourly time steps. It includes electricity, heating, cooling, transport, industry and desalination demands. For production it includes various types of power plants, variable renewable energy sources and combined heat and power plants. The main focus is to be able to simulate smart energy systems, and therefore includes modelling of electricity, district heating and gas grids. It allows for many types of P2X applications both for heating, gas and liquid fuels.

Developer:
Sustainable Energy Planning Group, Aalborg University

Related model documentation:
- [IAM PARIS model page](https://iamparis.eu/models/22)

Description:
The EU-TIMES model, is the multi-region, European version of TIMES, which is designed for analysing the role of energy technologies and their innovation needs for meeting European policy targets related to energy and climate change. It models technologies uptake and deployment and their interaction with the energy infrastructure in an energy systems perspective.

E4SMA

| Conversation | c42 |

**Full answer**

### EnergyPLAN

The loaded profile describes its purpose as follows:
EnergyPLAN is an input-output model that simulates the annual operation of the entire energy system in hourly time steps. It includes electricity, heating, cooling, transport, industry and desalination demands. For production it includes various types of power plants, variable renewable energy sources and combined heat and power plants. The main focus is to be able to simulate smart energy systems, and therefore includes modelling of electricity, district heating and gas grids. It allows for many types of P2X applications both for heating, gas and liquid fuels.

Related model documentation:
- [IAM PARIS model page](https://iamparis.eu/models/22)

Description:
The EU-TIMES model, is the multi-region, European version of TIMES, which is designed for analysing the role of energy technologies and their innovation needs for meeting European policy targets related to energy and climate change. It models technologies uptake and deployment and their interaction with the energy infrastructure in an energy systems perspective.

E4SMA
